result.markdown: --- title: "Applied replication for data skills" subtitle: "Short session – the EU-frames case" format: revealjs # The runs that core-runs.lua would lift into the main flow. This deck has no # optional run and no deck map: every slide is shown. core-runs: [] --- ## {#today .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.todaymeta} A short session in two halves, with one break, on the EU-frames case ::: :::: {.todaybox} ::: {.nonincremental .fs-85} 1. The claim and its reproduction – three kinds of repetition, Multi100 from the inside, the paper and its record, the estimand statement, and a recorded result reproduced 2. The multiverse of the claim – the specification menu, your own tries on the class chart, the curve of 864 and how to read it, and the replication with new data ::: :::: ::: {.todaytake .fs-85} You leave with an estimand statement, a reproduced result, and your own place among the 864 justifiable analyses of the claim ::: ::: {.todaymeta} Everything runs in the browser lab, nothing to install ::: ::: notes Welcome. Two halves, one break, and one published claim throughout: a study of what the European Union means to the people of its member states, and of whether the economic crisis changed that. In the first half I give you the vocabulary of three kinds of repetition, show you Multi100 from the inside, as one of the five analysts who reanalysed this claim, then the paper itself and what SCORE found when it checked it. You write down the question that the claim answers, and before the break you reproduce the result that one of the analysts recorded. In the second half you become the sixth analyst: you take the analysis apart into its decisions, try alternatives in the browser lab, put the one that you would defend on the class chart, and we read the class against every justifiable analysis of these data. Nothing needs installing. ::: ## What you do not need {#what-you-do-not-need} ::: {.none} - No installation: the browser lab runs R inside a tab of your browser, with the data in place - No git, and no GitHub account - No OSF account – we read the OSF as readers, without logging in - Nothing leaves your machine except the one result that you choose to send to the class chart ::: ::: {.fragment} **Do this now:** open the browser lab in a tab and leave it to load. R loads in the page while we talk; once it has, run the three cells of Task 1. ::: ::: {.urlbox .fragment} [{{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/lab.html]({{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/lab.html) ::: ::: notes Before anything else, what you do not need. You do not need to have installed anything: the browser lab runs R inside a tab of your browser, with the data already there. You do not need git, a GitHub account or an OSF account, because we read the OSF from the outside. The one thing that leaves your machine today is the single result that you choose to send to the class chart. [advance] One thing to do right now, while I talk. Open the browser lab at the address on the screen and leave the tab alone; R takes a while to load there, longer on a slow connection. Once the first cell shows a Run Code button, run the three cells of Task 1, which check that the panel is there. If the page will not load, try another browser, and tell me. ::: # FIRST HALF – The claim and its reproduction {#first-half-the-claim-and-its-reproduction .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} First half ::: ::: notes The first half. I start with the vocabulary of three kinds of repetition, from the glossary that the SCORE programme published, and with the Multi100 project from the inside, because I was one of the five analysts who reanalysed the claim that we work on. Then the paper itself: the survey question behind it, the scales, the panel that you have in your browser, the model and the claim, and what SCORE found when it tried to reproduce and to replicate the study. You write the question that the claim answers, in one sentence, and we read the class at once. And before the break you reproduce the result that one of two analysts recorded, to the third decimal, and find out why your number is exactly that number and why the other group has another one. ::: ## Three kinds of repetition {#three-kinds-of-repetition} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](eu-frames-short_files/figure-revealjs/matrix-short-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ::: {.src} @AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen; @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms ::: ::: notes Here is the vocabulary of the session as one grid, in the words of the glossary that Nosek and colleagues wrote for the SCORE programme. The question stays the same throughout, and what varies is the data and the analysis. The same data and the same analysis is reproducibility: if I rerun your recipe, do I get your number? The same data under a different, justifiable analysis is robustness, which asks whether your finding survives my defensible choices. The same analysis on new data is replicability. The fourth cell, new data and a new analysis at once, is generalisability, and we leave it aside. Everything that follows refers back to this grid. You reproduce a result before the break, you spend the second half on robustness, and we end on a replication of this very paper. ::: ## Multi100 from the inside {#multi100-from-the-inside .smaller} ::: {.small} - Multi100 gave one claim from each of 100 published studies to at least five independent analysts, and I was one of the five on this claim - What arrived: the **published paper** in full, its **central claim** in one sentence, and a pointer to the **data**, sixteen Eurobarometer waves that each analyst fetched from GESIS under licence. No instruction on method - **Task 1**, a free reanalysis ending in one categorical conclusion; months later **Task 2**, one main result under four instructions: a single test statistic, the contextual variables of the paper set aside, the **positive non-materialist form of EU framing** as the outcome and the **unemployment rate** as the predictor - Every statistic was converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a **Cohen's *d***, so that five models in two software languages could be read on one axis ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Two things stayed hidden throughout: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**. ::: ::: {.src} @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; the Multi100 preregistration, osf.io/4ev9t, pp. 4–8. ::: ::: notes Multi100 took one claim from each of a hundred published studies and gave it to at least five independent analysts, and I was one of the five on this claim. What arrived was the paper, the claim in one sentence lifted from the abstract, and a pointer to the data, sixteen Eurobarometer waves that each analyst fetched from GESIS under licence. No instruction on method: any analysis that you could defend. The work came in two tasks: a free reanalysis ending in one categorical verdict, and months later one main result under four instructions, which fixed the outcome and the predictor, set aside the contextual variables of the paper, and left everything else to us. Every statistic was then converted to a partial correlation and a Cohen's d, so that five models could be read on one axis. [advance] And two things stayed hidden: who the others were, and what they were finding. ::: ## The five results {#the-five-results .smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](eu-frames-short_files/figure-revealjs/forest5-1.png){width=912} ::: ::: ::: {.small} - All five estimates negative, with partial *r* from **−0.45 to −0.06** on the degrees of freedom of each inference, and one of the five not significant even by the errors of its own model - Multi100 recorded PRL47 at *r* = −0.006 (open circle), because its *z* was converted on 394,575 respondents ::: ::: {.src} Task 2 results as recorded in the public Multi100 dataset (osf.io/q5h2c); PRL47 placed on the 404.5 Satterthwaite df of a course refit of its design (cases/eu-frames/data/reference_marks.csv). ::: ::: notes Here are the five of us, on this one claim. All five found a negative association, so on direction we were unanimous. On size: from minus point zero six at the top, which is not significant even by the errors of its own model, to minus point four five, more than seven times as large. The orange dot is me, at minus point two four. Now the open circle on the row of PRL47, the value that Multi100 recorded, minus point zero zero six, because its z statistic was converted on the number of respondents, as if every respondent were an independent test of a national unemployment rate. The filled dot puts the same statistic on the degrees of freedom of a refit of its design, close to my own result. As recorded, the spread looked like two orders of magnitude, mostly from the conversion; the rest is what the second half is about. ::: ## The question and the items {#the-question-and-the-items .smaller} ::: {.small} - The **Standard Eurobarometer**: face-to-face interviews in every member state, about a thousand per country in each wave, a new sample every time, archived by GESIS - One question, **"What does the European Union mean to you personally?"**, with a card of fourteen meanings; every item that the respondent picks is recorded - The original author (OA) set the 'Euro' aside and sorted the other thirteen into four framing scales, which cross the valence of a meaning with its content: ::: ::: {.fs-70} | Dimension | Items, with the pooled share of respondents who mentioned each | |:--|:--| | Cosmopolitan (positive, non-materialist) | Peace (28.54%), Democracy (21.86%), Freedom to travel, study and work anywhere in the EU (50.99%), Cultural diversity (22.12%), Stronger say in the world (23.14%) | | Utilitarian (positive, materialist) | Economic prosperity (18.66%), Social protection (11.93%) | | Communitarian (negative, non-materialist) | Loss of our cultural identity (12.06%), More crime (17.50%), Not enough control at external borders (16.61%), Unemployment (16.64%) | | Libertarian (negative, materialist) | Bureaucracy (21.51%), Waste of money (21.64%) | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} A scale is a **share of mentions**: "the sum of the mentioned items belonging to the specific framing dimension, divided by the total number of items mentioned by the respondent" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623] ::: ::: notes The data are the Standard Eurobarometer, the survey of the European Commission: face-to-face interviews, about a thousand per country in each wave, and a fresh sample every time, so that we read change in populations and never in persons. The outcome of the paper comes from one question with a card: what does the European Union mean to you personally? The interviewer reads out fourteen meanings, and every one that the respondent picks is recorded. The original author, whom I call OA from here on, set the euro aside and sorted the other thirteen into four scales that cross the valence of a meaning with its content; the cosmopolitan scale is the one that Multi100 named. [advance] And a scale is a share: the items of a dimension that you mention, divided by everything that you mention. Hold on to that definition, because several decisions of the second half are about it. ::: ## The scales and the panel {#the-scales-and-the-panel .smaller} ::: {.small} - **16 waves, 2004–2013**, the crisis decade, in the **27** member states of the time; OA modelled about **390,000** respondents in three levels, respondents in country-waves in countries - The course works on the **country-year panel**: the four scales averaged within each country and year, **270 country-years** built from **416,698** respondents, with the national **unemployment rate** and **GDP growth** beside them ::: ::: {.fs-70} | Column | What it is | |:--|:--| | `cntry`, `year` | the cell | | `mcosmo`, `mutil`, `mcomm`, `mlib` | the four framing scales, averaged in the cell, 0–1 | | `mpos`, `mneg` | the two composites: all positive items, all negative items | | `unemp`, `growth` | national unemployment rate and GDP growth, World Bank series | | `n_cy` | the respondents behind the cell, from 500 to 3,614 | | `bailout` | 1 if an EU/IMF assistance programme was running | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The panel addresses the **contextual** question, whether the framing of a country moves with its unemployment; the **compositional** one, whether the same people changed or the mix of people did, needs the respondents. ::: ::: {.src} @Teney2016DoesEUEconomic [pp. 622–625]; `cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy.csv`, with its codebook. ::: ::: notes Sixteen waves between 2004 and 2013, in the twenty-seven member states of the time, and about three hundred and ninety thousand respondents, whom OA modelled in three levels. The Eurobarometer files are licensed by GESIS and may not be passed on, so the course works on an aggregate that I built from them and may share: the four scales averaged within each country and year, two hundred and seventy country-years from more than four hundred thousand interviews, with the national unemployment rate and GDP growth beside them. This is the file that the browser lab has loaded for you. Note the column `n_cy`, the respondents behind each cell, because whether a cell should count by its people is one of the decisions of the second half. [advance] One limit to say plainly: a panel of country means answers the contextual question, and cannot tell whether the same people changed or the mix of people did. ::: ## The model and the claim {#the-model-and-the-claim .smaller} ::: {.claimcard} "… poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" Teney (2016: 619), the claim as Multi100 gave it to the analysts ::: ::: {.small} - The hypothesis of the paper reads differently: "Poor national economic performances significantly increase the negative and decrease the positive EU-framing dimensions. The effect is stronger on the materialist dimensions of EU framing" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 621] - **Model 1** of Table 3: unemployment on the cosmopolitan scale, **b = −0.00340, t = −4.03, p < .001**, in a three-level model with sex, age, education, occupation, type of community, GDP growth, and the interactions of each economic indicator with education - **Model 2** adds the variables on EU policies and party positions, and the same coefficient falls to **−0.00138, t = −1.54** ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Within one paper, support for the claim depends on which of the two models you read, and the paper reports both. ::: ::: {.src} @Teney2016DoesEUEconomic [pp. 619, 621, 626–627]. ::: ::: notes This is the claim as every Multi100 analyst received it, cut from the abstract. The hypothesis of the paper itself reads differently, in two parts, and the second part, about the materialist dimensions, never reached us. Which sentence of a paper gets tested is a decision that somebody makes before any analyst opens the data. The number behind the claim is one coefficient from Model 1 of Table 3: unemployment on the cosmopolitan scale, minus point zero zero three four, with a t of minus four, inside a three-level model with individual controls, GDP growth and education interactions. Model 2 adds the variables on EU policies and party positions, and the same coefficient falls to less than half and loses significance. [advance] So inside the original study the claim already rests on a choice between two models, and the paper reports both. ::: ## The record in SCORE {#the-record-in-score .smaller} ::: {.small} SCORE put the paper through every kind of repetition on the grid: - **Reproduction**, with the Stata code that OA supplied on request: the push-button attempt failed before it produced a number, because the file names in the code did not match the files available for download, and the attempt that rebuilt the data from source was recorded as **'not reproduced'** - **Robustness**: the five Multi100 reanalyses that you have just met, unanimous on direction and more than sevenfold apart in size - **Replication**, on fourteen later Standard Eurobarometer waves fielded between 2013 and 2019: verdict **'not successful'** by the criterion that SCORE set in advance, a negative coefficient significant at 5% ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Three verdicts on one paper, one for each cell of the grid. The one that five careful people disagreed about is the one that we can work on today. ::: ::: {.src} The SCORE dossier on the paper, [osf.io/h7432](https://osf.io/h7432); @MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial. ::: ::: notes SCORE put this paper through every cell of the grid, all of it public at the address on the slide. The reproduction first. OA supplied the two Stata do-files when asked, but could not share the data, because the GESIS terms forbid it. The push-button attempt failed before it produced a number, because the file names in the code did not match the files that you can download, and the attempt that rebuilt the data from source could not recover the published effect size, so it was recorded as not reproduced. Robustness is the Multi100 study: one sign, sizes more than sevenfold apart. And a replication on fourteen later Standard Eurobarometer waves was judged not successful by the criterion that SCORE had set in advance. [advance] Three verdicts on one paper. The middle one is where five careful people disagreed, and it is the one that we can work on. ::: ## The questions of the five analysts {#five-analysts-five-questions .smaller} ::: {.fs-70} | Analyst | Level of analysis in Task 2 | Estimator in Task 2 | Question of the free phase | |:--|:--|:--|:--| | 018OL | 420 cells of country, year and wave | random intercepts for country, year and wave | GDP per capita on the mean of the seven positive items | | KEVF1 | 209,826 respondents | random intercepts for countries and years within countries | GDP growth on the sum of the seven positive items | | PRL47 | 394,575 respondents | three levels, random slopes, individual and national controls | GDP per capita, growth and a crisis dummy on three positive shares | | KQXUE | 270 country-years | a fixed effect for each country | GDP growth and unemployment on the cosmopolitan and utilitarian shares | | **C6HJR** | 270 country-years | fixed effects for country and year | GDP growth and unemployment on the share of the seven positive items | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} - Five free analyses, five different questions, and **one shared verdict**, 'evidence for the claim'; three of the five never used the unemployment rate - Analysts who look as though they disagree are often answering different questions, which is why Lundberg and colleagues ask every study "What is your estimand?" [@LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand] ::: ::: {.src} The Multi100 record (osf.io/q5h2c) and the public code of the analysts, read on the [case page]({{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/index.html#sec-reanalysts); @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial on the red-card study. ::: ::: notes Before you write your own, look at what the five of us did in the free first task. GDP per capita for one, GDP growth for another, GDP measures with a crisis dummy for a third, and three of the five never touched the unemployment rate. The outcomes differ too, a mean, a sum, a share, three separate shares, and so do the units: two of us on respondents, one on cells of a country in one wave, two on country-years. Those are five different questions, and every one of us recorded the same verdict, evidence for the claim. [advance] Auspurg and Brüderl found the same thing in the twenty-nine teams of the red-card study: much of what looks like analytical disagreement is unstated disagreement about what is being estimated. Lundberg and colleagues put the remedy in the title of their paper, what is your estimand, and that is what you write now. ::: ## The estimand statement {#the-estimand-statement} ::: {.claimcard} "The expected change in [unit quantity] among [target population] for a 1-percentage-point difference in unemployment, holding [assumptions] fixed." ::: ::: {.small} - Unit quantity – a *person's* cosmopolitan framing, or a *country-year* mean? - Target population – which countries, which years? - Held fixed – the stable traits of a country, the shocks of a year, the other measure of the economy? ::: ::: {.fragment} **Now:** your one-sentence estimand for the claim. Write it, hold it, and send it when I say go. ::: ::: {.src} The template follows @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand. ::: ::: notes Fill in the brackets of the statement on the slide: your one-sentence estimand for the claim. Is the unit quantity the framing of a person or the mean of a country-year? Which countries and years are the population? What do you hold fixed: the stable traits of a country, whatever every country went through in a year, the other measure of the economy? Write it, hold it, and send it when I say go. [go; read three or four aloud] Look at the spread. Some of you wrote about the framing of a person, some about a country-year average, some named different years or different things held fixed. None of those statements is wrong. They are different questions, and the coefficient means something different in each: the disagreement of the five free analyses in miniature. Keep your statement for the second half. ::: ## Hands-on 1 – The reproduction {#hands-on-1-the-reproduction .smaller} ::: {.small} **Task 3 in the browser lab.** Choose one of two analysts, run their cells in order, and reach the value on record. Every cell with gaps to fill has a hint and a full solution beneath it. | Analyst | Data | Model | Recorded by Multi100 | |:--|:--|:--|:--| | C6HJR | the course panel, 270 country-years | fixed effects for country and year, conventional standard errors | t = −3.804 on 233 df | | KQXUE | `analyst_KQXUE.csv`, 270 country-years rebuilt from the code of the analyst | a fixed effect for each country, conventional standard errors | t = −7.169 on 242 df | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} When you have your value, write the analyst and the *t*, for example `KQXUE t = -7.169`, hold it, and send it when I say go. If you finish early, take the other analyst. ::: ::: {.urlbox .fragment} [{{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/lab.html#task-3-reproduction]({{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/lab.html#task-3-reproduction) ::: ::: notes Now you work, on the question at the heart of reproducibility: given the data and the model, does the recorded number come back? Open Task 3 in the browser lab and choose one of two analysts. Mine runs on the course panel, with fixed effects for country and year. KQXUE built a panel of its own, which the course rebuilt from the Stata code that the analyst deposited, and gave each country a fixed effect and no year effects. Each analyst has a few cells, one step to a cell, and every gap has a hint and a solution underneath; using them is not cheating. The page offers a third analyst, whose first cell downloads two large packages; leave that one for later. When you have your value, write the analyst and the t, hold it, and send it when I say go. [circulate; then go] ::: ## Reproducibility and analytical choice {#the-same-t-within-an-analyst} :::: {.none} ::: {.fragment} Everyone who chose the same analyst got **the same *t***, to the third decimal, on different machines. That is reproducibility, and once the data and the code are in hand it is the cheap R. ::: ::: {.fragment} The two analysts did not get the same *t*: −3.804 and −7.169, on one claim, under one set of instructions. ::: ::: {.fragment} Neither was careless. The numbers differ because the two made different choices about the **data** (which unemployment series, which respondents), the **model** (which fixed effects) and the **code** (one wave appended twice). ::: :::: ::: notes Look at what just happened. Everyone who chose the same analyst landed on the same number, to the third decimal, on different machines. [advance] Now look across the two groups. Minus three point eight and minus seven point two, for one claim, from two analysts who were given the same four instructions. [advance] Neither was careless. The numbers differ because of choices. About the data: KQXUE measured unemployment as a share of the whole population aged twenty to sixty-four, not of the labour force, and left out the respondents who mentioned nothing, where I scored them zero. About the model: a fixed effect for each country but none for the year, where mine has both. About the code: the Stata script appended one wave twice, and my own first build read one wave twice too, corrected before Multi100 recorded the value. Such choices are what robustness, the second R, is about. ::: ## Three models side by side {#three-models-side-by-side .smaller} ::: {.small} | Analyst | Model | What it compares | Conventional *t* | |:--|:--|:--|:--| | C6HJR | fixed effects for country and year | each country with itself, after the change common to all countries in a year | −3.804 on 233 df | | KQXUE | a fixed effect for each country | each country with itself, the common change included | −7.169 on 242 df | | 018OL | random intercepts for country, year and wave | change within countries and differences between them at once | −1.206 on 396.9 df | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Between the 27 country means the slope is +0.0041, within countries −0.0056: a model that blends the two comparisons, as random intercepts do, assumes them equal, and the within–between model rejects that (p = 0.024). ::: ::: {.src} Table and fragment as on the one-day deck (`_segments/eu-frames/_p3-three-models.qmd`); `cases/eu-frames/data/display_between_within.csv`. ::: ::: notes The two models that you reproduced are two of the three estimators that the menu is built around, beside the third, which the lab offers and we skipped. My model has fixed effects for country and for year, so each country is compared with itself net of whatever all of Europe went through in a year. KQXUE has a fixed effect for each country only, so the common change stays in the comparison. 018OL has random intercepts for country, year and wave, which use the change within countries and the differences between them. [advance] On this panel those two comparisons point in opposite directions: across the country means the slope is slightly positive, within countries it is negative, and the within–between model rejects the equality that random intercepts assume. That is one reason why the three t-values are so far apart, the decision that the second half calls the Estimator. ::: ## Twenty-seven clusters {#twenty-seven-clusters .smaller} ::: {.small} | Test | Two-way fixed effects (C6HJR) | Country fixed effects, on the course panel | |:--|:--|:--| | Conventional | t = −3.80 on 233 df, p = 0.0002 | t = −6.87 on 242 df | | Clustered by country, CR1 | t = −2.31 on 26 df, p = 0.029 | t = −3.62 on 26 df | | Clustered, CR2, Satterthwaite df | t = −2.23 on 9.8 df, p = 0.0504 | t = −3.51 on 8.5 df, p = 0.0072 | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The estimate is the same in every row; only the test changes. The years of one country are not independent, 27 countries are few clusters of unequal weight, and the CR2 test with Satterthwaite df, which classes every point of the curve, counts the countries that effectively carry the evidence. ::: ::: {.src} @BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard; @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust; `cases/eu-frames/data/display_inference.csv`, as on the one-day deck. ::: ::: notes Now the question that conventional errors avoid. Both reproduced t-values treat each row as independent evidence, but the years of one country resemble each other. Clustering by country allows any pattern of correlation within a country, and the evidence then rests on twenty-seven countries rather than two hundred and seventy rows. With so few clusters, of very unequal weight, the usual clustered test is still too generous, so the course uses the CR2 correction, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom that count how many countries effectively carry the information, fewer than ten here. Read my row: the same estimate goes from a p of two in ten thousand to just above point zero five. Read the row of the design of KQXUE on the course panel: it stays significant under every test. [advance] The estimate never moves, only the test does, and the CR2 test classes every point of the curve. ::: ## Break {.darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} The return time is posted\ Keep the browser lab open in its tab ::: ::: notes Break, and the return time is posted. Keep the browser lab open in its tab, because the second half carries on there and the page forgets everything that you ran if you close it. If your reproduction did not come out, come and find me now, and we will sort it out before we start again. ::: # SECOND HALF – The multiverse of the claim {#second-half-the-multiverse-of-the-claim .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Second half ::: ::: notes Welcome back. In the first half you reproduced a recorded number. Now you become the sixth analyst and make choices of your own. I open the menu of the fourteen decisions that any analysis of this claim has to take, with the survey decisions first, because this audience knows that part of the menu best, and show you the code behind the menu. Then you work the menu in the browser lab, one decision at a time, and send the analysis that you would defend to the class chart. We read the class against the curve of every justifiable analysis of these data, ask which decision moves the estimates most, and what such a curve can and cannot establish. We end with the critics, with what a preregistration would have added, and with the replication of this claim on new data. ::: ## The specification menu {#the-specification-menu .smaller} ::: {.small} Fourteen decisions stand between the panel and a verdict on the claim, in three groups. One test sorts them: **would two analysts who chose differently accept each other's number as an answer to the same question?** | Group | Decisions | A different choice | |:--|:--|:--| | **The question** | frame set, scoring rule, predictor, adjustment set, sample, whose average, estimator | changes what is estimated, so that two analysts answer different questions | | **Measurement** | respondents who mention nothing, item set, cell weighting, published series | changes how a named quantity is measured, and leaves the question as it is | | **The model** | predictor form, outcome family, inference | changes how the model is fitted and how sure its answer is said to be | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Every option of every decision was asked whether it is a justifiable way of answering *this* claim. The options that are cross into the **864 specifications** of the curve of the claim, and the [specification menu]({{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/menu.html) gives the reason for each option that is not. ::: ::: {.src} @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand; the specification menu and the [decision map]({{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/map.html) of the course site. ::: ::: notes Here is the menu. Fourteen decisions stand between the panel and a verdict on the claim. One test sorts them into three groups: would two analysts who chose differently accept each other's number as an answer to the same question? If not, the decision belongs to the question, and it rewrites the estimand statement that you wrote before the break. If they would, and the decision concerns how a named construct becomes a column of numbers, it is a measurement decision; everything else belongs to the model, which changes how the fit is made and how sure its answer is said to be. [advance] Every option was asked whether it is a justifiable way of answering this claim, and the options that passed cross into the eight hundred and sixty-four specifications of the curve. The menu page gives the reason for each option left off. ::: ## The survey decisions {#the-survey-decisions .smaller} ::: {.small} Six of the fourteen belong to survey methodology: - **Which items form a scale** – all 13, or the 12 without 'Unemployment', the item that ties the outcome to the predictor by its content. And which published series of unemployment, where four move together and a fifth, with no British row and almost nothing before 2009, changes the population while looking like a measure. ::: ## Estimator and inference {#estimator-and-inference .smaller} ::: {.fs-80} | Estimator | What it compares | Curve | |:--|:--|:--| | **Two-way fixed effects** | each country with itself, net of the change shared by all member states in a year | on | | **Country fixed effects** | each country with itself, the shared change included | on | | **Random effects** | a blend of the two comparisons, assuming country effects unrelated to the predictor | off – the assumption fails on this panel | | **Pooled OLS** | countries with each other *and* over time | off – another question | | **Within–between model** | the two comparisons, separately | off – a check, taught beside the curve | ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The two designs on the curve are two estimands: below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 are 92.6% of the specifications with country effects and 61.8% of the two-way ones. **Inference is fixed on the curve**: every point is classed by errors clustered by country with the CR2 correction, on Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, the test of the slide before the break. ::: ::: {.src} @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects; @BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard; @PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust; the [module on panel data]({{< var site-url >}}companion/panel-data.html). ::: ::: notes The Estimator moves the results most, and you met it before the break. Two-way fixed effects compare each country with itself and remove whatever all member states went through in a given year. Country fixed effects compare each country with itself and keep that shared change in. Both are defensible readings of the claim, so both stay on the curve, as two estimands rather than two ways of estimating one. Random effects blend the within and the between comparison and assume that stable country differences are unrelated to unemployment, which the test of the two slopes rejected. Pooled OLS mixes the two comparisons, which run in opposite directions here, and the within–between model separates them, as a check beside the curve. [circulate; keep the Multiverse page on the screen] ::: ## Where the idea comes from {#where-the-idea-comes-from .smaller} ::: {.small} - **Multiverse analysis** [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse] began with the choices made before any model is fitted, how to code, exclude and combine: build every dataset that a reasonable set of choices could have produced and run the analysis on all of them. The founding paper asks that "it should become standard practice to go beyond a single data set analysis and to acknowledge the multiverse of statistical results", and concedes that doing so "will often be difficult, and to a large extent subjective" (p. 710) - **Specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis] makes the same move for the choices of the model and adds a display, the estimates in order with the choices beneath each one, and a test of the curve as a whole against a null distribution built by permutation - Behind both stands the **garden of forking paths** [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]: one test chosen after looking at the data already has the wrong p-value, and a single path through the garden keeps no record of its branches ::: ::: {.fragment .small} What you did in Task 4 was to walk three or four paths of that garden and write them down, which every published analysis could do and almost none reports. ::: ::: notes A brief history, because the vocabulary is a mess and knowing which word came from where helps. Multiverse analysis is Steegen and colleagues in 2016, and it grew out of the choices made before any model is fitted, with the proposal that you build every dataset that a reasonable set of choices could have produced and report the whole set of results. The founding paper asks for that to become standard practice, and concedes in the same breath that it is difficult and to a large extent subjective, which the critics would later press. Specification curve analysis is Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, the same move for the choices of the model, with a display and, in its full form, a test of the whole curve. Behind both stands the garden of forking paths of Gelman and Loken. [advance] In Task 4 you walked three or four paths of that garden and wrote them down. ::: ## Enumeration and curation {#enumeration-and-curation .smaller} ::: {.small} Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask what a multiverse is *for*, and name three uses, "as a tool for reflection and critique, as a persuasive tool, as a serious inferential tool"; it "fails as a persuasive tool when researchers disagree about which variations should be included in the analysis", and "fails as a serious inferential tool when the included analyses do not target a coherent estimand" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1] - **Enumerate**: cross every option of every decision. Complete and mechanical, and the set fills with specifications that nobody would defend, so that the spread stops meaning anything. Our fourteen decisions multiplied out give about **1,728,000** specifications, each testable under several inference rules - **Curate**: keep only what you would defend in print, for an estimand that you have named. The set becomes a claim of its own, which a sceptic can attack option by option, so the reasons go beside the curve ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The curve of the claim is a curated **864**: every option was asked whether it answers *this* claim in a justifiable way, because "there is nothing in the distribution of estimates per se that tells us which is the true effect" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 119] ::: ::: notes The question that organises the current debate is the one that Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask: what is a multiverse for? Reflection and critique, persuasion, or inference, and each purpose needs a differently built set. Enumerate, and you cross every option of every decision: complete, mechanical, and the set fills with specifications that nobody would defend, so that of course the answer varies; our fourteen decisions multiplied out give about one point seven million specifications. Or curate, and keep only what you would defend in print for the estimand that you have named, which makes the set a claim of its own that a sceptic can attack option by option. That is what the curve of 864 does, and what Multi100 did for its 504 reanalyses, with no inferential statistics anywhere in its paper - **Inference** – ask whether the curve *as a whole* is surprising if there were no association at all. The first is description: showing how the estimate moves as the choices move. That is what we built, and it is all that Multi100 did for its five hundred and four reanalyses, whose paper carries no inferential statistics. The second is inference: asking whether the curve, taken as a whole, is more extreme than you would expect if there were no association. Most published curves stop before it. [advance] Four things are missing from so tidy a chart. The options that the audit left off, and the specifications that nobody ran, such as a person-level model. A curve is a map of the menu that was written for it. ::: ## Dependence among the estimates {#not-864-tests .smaller} ::: {.small} - Every specification reuses the **same 270 country-years**, so the estimates share their noise: '77.2% below zero with CR2 p < 0.05' **describes** the curve and is not a p-value for the claim. Clustered errors allow for the years of one country within each fit, and clustering does not make the fits independent of one another - A test of the whole curve has to build its own null: **shuffle the unemployment and growth series of each country in time**, jointly, refit all 864 specifications, repeat **B = 500** times, and set the observed curve among the 500 null curves - With B = 500 the smallest reportable p is 2/(B + 1) ≈ 0.004, a floor set by the number of draws, and near p = 0.05 the Monte Carlo error is about ±0.01, so p = 0.04 and p = 0.06 are the same finding - [A DESIGN, NOT YET RUN]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"}, fixed before it runs, which is the position that a preregistration puts you in ::: ::: {.fragment .small} **Discussion.** The cosmopolitan scale alone, the outcome that Multi100 instructed, has 288 specifications on the curve: **94.4% below zero, 65.6% below zero with CR2 p < 0.05.** Strong evidence? *Against what null?* ::: ::: {.src} @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis; @PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues; the [reading on the specification curve]({{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/reading-inference.html), which sets out the design in full. ::: ::: notes Seventy-seven per cent lie below zero with a CR2 p under point zero five. But all of them use the same two hundred and seventy country-years, so they share their noise: sampling luck that pushed a few country-years the way of the claim pushed hundreds of specifications with them. The percentage describes the curve; it is not a test of the claim. A test of the whole curve needs a null, built by hand: shuffle the economic series of each country in time, refit the whole curve, five hundred times. The smallest reportable p is then about point zero zero four, and near the threshold the Monte Carlo error is a point either way. The badge says that this test is designed and not run. [harvest; the target answer: we cannot say until we know what chance produces on these dependent data] ::: ## Critics of the multiverse {#the-critics .smaller} ::: {.small} - **The pruning critique.** "Multiverse analyses are only informative when all included models represent equally plausible strategies for estimating the same estimand" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1], written in reply to a study of 3.6 billion estimates [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources]; in the red-card study, Auspurg and Brüderl had traced most of the disagreement among the 29 teams to four different estimands [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial] - **One correct analysis.** Once the auxiliary assumptions are fixed, "there is a fact of the matter about which analysis correctly implements that test" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 7], and "Scientists should not compute the percentage of agreement across different data-analytic strategies, because we do not resolve scientific disagreement by majority vote" (p. 16) - **What is it for?** "as a tool for reflection and critique, as a persuasive tool, as a serious inferential tool" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1], each needing a differently built set ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The curve of the claim is built as the first critic asks, pruned to one claim with a published reason for every option, and it stops short of the second: it keeps **two estimators as two estimands**, because the claim as written does not say whether the change shared by all of Europe belongs to the comparison. The decomposition by decision is the one use that every party endorses, since it shows where the argument has to happen. ::: ::: {.src} Quotations from the preprints, by their own pagination, as in the [module on the multiverse and its critics]({{< var site-url >}}companion/multiverse.html). ::: ::: notes Katrin Auspurg, who with Josef Brüderl traced the red-card spread to four different questions, replied to a study of three point six billion estimates with the sentence at the top of the slide: a multiverse is informative only when every model in it is an equally plausible way of estimating the same estimand. Lakens and colleagues go further: once the assumptions are fixed, one analysis implements the test, so a wide spread is evidence that most of the specifications estimate something else, and counting the share that agree settles nothing. Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask what a multiverse is for and name three uses. [advance] Our curve follows the first critic, pruned to one claim with a reason beside every option, and stops short of the second, because it keeps two estimators as two estimands. Every party endorses the decomposition, which shows where the argument has to happen. ::: ## What preregistration settles {#what-preregistration-settles .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.small} **It does settle** - That your specification was not chosen *because of* its result - That your rule for what counts as support was fixed before you had a result - That a reader can tell what you intended from what you changed ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.small} **It does not settle** - Whether the specification was any good - Whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies - Whether the assumptions behind it hold A badly reasoned analysis that is preregistered is still badly reasoned; the preregistration adds a timestamp ::: ::: :::: ::: {.fragment .small} Today you explored and said so: the chart labels every dot of the class **exploratory**. Task 5 of the one-day workshop on this case adds the declaration, one specification fixed before it runs, with a reason that a causal graph supports, because "in the absence of preregistration, researchers may as well determine what is equivalent based on whether or not it supports their result" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 5] ::: ::: notes So where does preregistration fit? It settles a limited set of things, and the two columns matter equally. On the left: that your specification was not chosen because of its result, that your rule for support was fixed before you had a result, and that a reader can tell what you intended from what you changed. No other device provides those guarantees. On the right, what it does not settle: whether the specification was any good, whether it estimates the quantity that your question implies, or whether its assumptions hold. A badly reasoned analysis that is preregistered is still badly reasoned, with a timestamp on it. [advance] Today you explored, and the chart says so on every dot. The one-day workshop adds the other half, a specification declared before it runs, with a reason from a causal graph: the declaration protects the choice, and the reasoning justifies it. ::: ## Replication with new data {#replication-with-new-data .smaller} ::: {.small} - A replication asks **the same question of new data**. The Standard Eurobarometer kept asking what the EU means to people after 2013, and SCORE commissioned a replication on fourteen Standard waves fielded between 2013 and 2019, with a model close to that of the original study - Its verdict: **not successful**, by the criterion that SCORE fixed in advance. A failed replication says that the claim did not hold in those data with that analysis; on its own it cannot say whether the data, the analysis or the world had changed ::: ::: {.fragment .fs-75} | Decision | Fixed before anyone opens the new data | |:--|:--| | **The claim and its test** | which coefficient, which sign, which threshold counts as success | | **The data** | which waves, which countries, which unemployment series | | **The measurement** | the fifteenth meaning on the answer card since the end of 2019; the respondents who mention nothing | | **The analysis** | the model of your analyst, as you reproduced it, unchanged | | **The report** | what you will say if the result differs, and what if it agrees | ::: ::: {.src} The SCORE dossier on the paper, [osf.io/h7432](https://osf.io/h7432); @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial. ::: ::: notes The last of the three Rs is replication: the same question, new data. The Standard Eurobarometer kept asking people what the EU means to them after 2013, and SCORE commissioned exactly this: fourteen Standard waves fielded between 2013 and 2019, and a model like that of the original author. The verdict was not successful, by the criterion that SCORE had set before the data were opened. It says that the claim did not hold in those data with that analysis, and not which of the three moved: the data, the analysis, or the world. [advance] A replication of the analysis that you reproduced involves decisions of five kinds, and every one can be fixed before you look at the new data: the coefficient, sign and threshold; the waves, countries and series; the fifteenth answer category and the silent respondents; the model, unchanged; and what you will say either way. ::: ## The three Rs on this paper {#the-three-rs-on-this-paper} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](eu-frames-short_files/figure-revealjs/matrix-this-paper-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ::: {.src} The SCORE dossier on the paper, [osf.io/h7432](https://osf.io/h7432); the grid after @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms. ::: ::: notes The grid of the first half, with this paper written into its cells. Reproduction, the same data under the same analysis, failed twice before any question of the finding arose. Robustness, the same data under different justifiable analyses, is the Multi100 study, five analysts with one sign and sizes more than sevenfold apart, and since today it is also the class, on the curve of eight hundred and sixty-four. Replication, new data under the analysis of the original study, was not successful. Read the two lower cells against each other. Robustness asks whether the finding survives other defensible analyses of the data in hand, and here almost every justifiable analysis points the way of the claim, with the strength of the evidence depending on the estimator. Replicability asks whether the finding holds in new data under the original analysis, and here it did not. The two verdicts answer different questions, and neither settles the other. ::: ## What you take with you {#what-you-take-with-you} :::: {.none} ::: {.fragment .fadeInUp} You wrote the estimand behind a published claim, reproduced one of the results recorded for it to the third decimal, and can say why the two analysts differ. ::: ::: {.fragment .fadeInUp} You varied one decision at a time, put the analysis that you would defend on the class chart, and read your own place among 864 justifiable analyses of the same data. ::: ::: {.fragment .fadeInUp} A curve describes every justifiable analysis of the data in hand; a test of the whole curve, an analysis declared before it runs, and a replication on new data are the steps that it leaves to others. ::: :::: ::: notes Three sentences to take with you. You wrote the estimand behind a published claim, reproduced one of the results recorded for it to the third decimal, and you can say why the other group in this class got another number: different choices about the data, the model and the code, none of them careless. You then became the sixth analyst, varied one decision at a time, put the analysis that you would defend on the class chart, and read your own place among eight hundred and sixty-four justifiable analyses of the same data, which is a publishable way to report a robustness check. And you know what that curve is and is not. It describes every justifiable analysis of the data in hand, and it is only as good as the menu written for it; a test of the whole curve, a declared analysis and a replication on new data are steps that it leaves to others. ::: ## Where to go next {#where-to-go-next .smaller} ::: {.small} - **After the session**, the page of this track: what to reread, what to try in the browser lab with the time that you have, and where the rest of the course goes - **The companion modules** of the case, each written from its data: [The multiverse and its critics]({{< var site-url >}}companion/multiverse.html), [The items behind the scales]({{< var site-url >}}companion/measurement.html), [Weights]({{< var site-url >}}companion/weighting.html), [Panel data]({{< var site-url >}}companion/panel-data.html) and [Meta-analysis]({{< var site-url >}}companion/meta-analysis.html) - **The longer formats**: the [one-day workshop]({{< var site-url >}}tracks/eu-frames-one-day/index.html), which adds the causal graph and the preregistered analysis, and the [Extended course]({{< var site-url >}}tracks/eu-frames-extended/index.html), which takes the methods to the respondents - **Read**: @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand; @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial; @RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood; and the paper itself, @Teney2016DoesEUEconomic ::: ::: {.urlbox} [{{< var site-url >}}tracks/eu-frames-short/after.html]({{< var site-url >}}tracks/eu-frames-short/after.html) ::: ::: {.small} Everything is on the course site, and everything is open. ::: ::: notes Where to go from here. The page of this track called After the session, at the address on the screen, says what to reread, what to try in the browser lab, and where the rest of the course goes. The companion modules of the case are written from these data: the debate about the multiverse, with the quotations and page numbers that I only read to you today; the thirteen items behind the four scales; the weights, within cells and across cells; panel data, up to the within–between model; and meta-analysis, which puts the five analysts on one scale in full. The two things that the short session leaves out, the causal graph and the preregistered analysis, are in the one-day workshop on this case, and the Extended course takes the methods to the respondents. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
